1. Give yourself sixteen to twenty weeks. Half marathon fitness is built, not conjured, and rushing a plan into eight or ten weeks is the single most common reason first-timers end up injured or exhausted on race day. A longer runway lets you build volume gradually, absorb a bad week without panicking, and still arrive undertrained rather than overtrained, which is the safer place to be.

2. Follow the ten percent rule for mileage. Increase your total weekly distance by roughly ten percent at most from one week to the next, and build in a lighter step-back week every third or fourth week. Your cardiovascular system adapts faster than your tendons, ligaments and bones, and it is almost always the connective tissue that fails first when mileage climbs too quickly.

3. Get fitted for proper running shoes. Visit a specialist running shop and get your gait assessed rather than guessing your size and picking whatever looks fastest on the shelf. The right shoe for your foot shape and stride can be the difference between finishing comfortably and nursing blisters or shin pain for the last five miles.

4. Make your long run the anchor of the week. One run, growing steadily longer over the weeks, teaches your body to burn fat efficiently, strengthens the specific muscles used in sustained running, and builds the mental resilience of simply being on your feet for two hours or more. Everything else in the plan supports this one session.

5. Respect your easy days. It feels unproductive to run slowly, but easy runs done at a genuinely conversational pace let you recover, build aerobic capacity, and arrive at your harder sessions and long runs actually able to do them justice. Most new runners run their easy days too hard and their hard days too easy, which flattens all the benefit out of both.

6. Practise your fuelling strategy in training, never on race day. Try different gels, chews or sports drinks on your long runs so you know exactly what your stomach tolerates and roughly how often you need to take something in, typically every thirty to forty-five minutes once you're running past an hour. Race day is not the moment to discover that a particular gel gives you cramps.

7. Add strength training twice a week. Short sessions focused on your glutes, hips, core and calves build the stability that keeps your running form intact when you're tired in the closing miles. You don't need a gym membership or heavy weights; bodyweight squats, lunges, planks and calf raises done consistently make a real difference.

8. Learn to run by effort, not just pace. GPS watches are useful but wind, hills, heat and fatigue all change what a given pace actually costs you on a given day. Training yourself to recognise easy, moderate and hard effort by breathing and perceived exertion means you can adjust sensibly when conditions on race day don't match your spreadsheet.

9. Rehearse race-day logistics in advance. Know exactly how you'll get to the start, where to park or which train to catch, when bag drop closes, and how long the queue for the toilets is likely to be. A stressful, rushed morning burns nervous energy you'll want later, so remove as many unknowns as you can before you even start running.

10. Don't wear anything new on race day. New shoes, new socks, a new shirt with a seam you've never tested for twelve miles, all of it is a gamble. Wear kit you've already run long distances in, and if you want new gear for the race, break it in on a training run at least two weeks beforehand.

11. Include some hill work, even on a flat course. Hill repeats build leg strength and running economy that transfer directly to flat, fast running, and they raise your heart rate without the joint impact of sprinting. Even a hilly race course becomes far less intimidating once your legs already know what sustained climbing feels like.

12. Practise negative splits on your long runs. Aim to run the second half of a long training run slightly faster than the first, which trains both the physical discipline of holding back early and the mental habit of finishing strong. Runners who go out too fast in the first three miles of a half marathon are the ones who suffer most in the last three.

13. Taper properly in the final two weeks. Cut your mileage down significantly while keeping a little intensity in short bursts, so your legs arrive at the start line rested rather than fatigued from a training block you're still recovering from. Resist the urge to squeeze in one more big session out of nerves; it will cost you more than it gives you.

14. Sort out your hydration plan before race week. Know whether the race provides water or sports drink at aid stations, and practise drinking from a cup while running if you've never done it, because it's a genuinely fiddly skill. Dehydration and overhydration are both real risks, so aim to drink to thirst rather than forcing down more than you need.

15. Deal with niggles immediately, not eventually. A tight calf or a sore knee that you run through for three more weeks because you don't want to lose training days usually turns into the injury that actually stops you racing. A few days of rest, some gentle stretching or a visit to a physio early on is far cheaper than the alternative.

16. Prioritise sleep during your training block. Your body does most of its adaptation and repair while you're asleep, not while you're running, and consistently short sleep undermines recovery, immune function and motivation all at once. Treat a good night's sleep before your key long runs with the same seriousness you'd give the run itself.

17. Break the race into mental chunks. Thirteen point one miles is a long way to hold in your head as a single block, so plan to think of it in stages, the first few miles settling in, the middle miles finding rhythm, and the last three or four as their own separate effort where you dig in. This makes the distance feel manageable rather than overwhelming.

18. Know your pacing plan and write it down. Decide roughly what pace per mile gets you to your goal, and consider writing the splits on your arm or wrist so you're not doing maths at mile ten when you're tired. Starting even ten or fifteen seconds per mile too fast in the excitement of the start line routinely costs far more time later.

19. Find a training partner or join a club. Running with other people, even just for one session a week, makes hard workouts feel easier, keeps you accountable on the mornings you'd rather stay in bed, and gives you somewhere to ask the questions that come up constantly when you're new to this. Shared miles also tend to be genuinely more enjoyable miles.

20. Study the course profile before race day. Know where the hills are, where the tight turns are, and roughly where you'll hit the halfway point, so nothing on the route catches you by surprise. A hill you knew was coming at mile nine feels very different to a hill you discover on your legs with no warning.

21. Expect a wall somewhere between mile nine and eleven. Even well-trained first-timers often hit a rough patch in the last quarter of the race where motivation and energy both dip sharply. Have a plan for it in advance, whether that's a mantra, breaking the remaining distance into smaller goals, or simply expecting the low patch to pass, because it usually does within a mile or two.

22. Set a realistic first-time goal, or none at all. There is real value in racing your first half marathon purely to finish strong and enjoy it, saving the serious time-chasing for your second attempt once you know what the distance actually demands of you. A goal built from your training paces rather than a number you'd simply like to see is far more likely to leave you satisfied.

23. Warm up properly before the start. A few minutes of easy jogging and some dynamic stretches or leg swings in the corral get your muscles ready and settle pre-race nerves, which matters more over thirteen miles than it might for a shorter race. Standing still and cold for forty minutes before the gun goes is not the ideal preparation it might feel like.

24. Plan your post-race recovery before you need it. Have warm clothes, food and something to drink ready for the moment you cross the line, because your body cools down fast once you stop moving and the immediate aftermath is a poor time to be making decisions. A short walk, some gentle stretching and a proper meal within a couple of hours all help you recover faster than collapsing on the sofa the second you get home.

25. Remember that finishing is the achievement. It's easy, surrounded by other people's times and social media splits, to lose sight of the fact that simply training consistently for months and completing thirteen point one miles under your own power is a genuinely significant thing to have done. Whatever the clock says when you cross that line, treat it as the first data point in a longer running story, not a verdict on the whole effort.

"""
A small self-contained arithmetic expression interpreter.

This module implements, from scratch and without any third-party
dependencies, the three classic stages of a tiny language
implementation:

    1. Tokenizer (a.k.a. lexer) - turns a raw string such as
       "2 + 3 * (4 - 1)" into a flat stream of Token objects.
    2. Recursive descent parser - turns that stream of tokens into
       an abstract syntax tree (AST) that reflects operator
       precedence (``*`` and ``/`` bind tighter than ``+`` and
       ``-``) and explicit parenthesisation.
    3. Evaluator - walks the AST and computes a single numeric
       result.

The supported grammar, in a slightly informal EBNF, is::

    expression := term (("+" | "-") term)*
    term       := factor (("*" | "/") factor)*
    factor     := INTEGER
                | "(" expression ")"
                | ("+" | "-") factor

Only integers, parentheses and the four basic arithmetic operators
(``+``, ``-``, ``*``, ``/``) are supported. Division always produces
a Python float, matching the behaviour of Python's own ``/``
operator.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from enum import Enum, auto
from typing import List, Union


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Tokenizer
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class TokenType(Enum):
    """The distinct kinds of token our tiny language can produce."""

    INTEGER = auto()
    PLUS = auto()
    MINUS = auto()
    STAR = auto()
    SLASH = auto()
    LPAREN = auto()
    RPAREN = auto()
    EOF = auto()


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Token:
    """A single lexical token.

    ``value`` is only meaningful for ``INTEGER`` tokens, where it
    holds the parsed integer value; for every other token type it is
    ``None``.
    """

    type: TokenType
    value: Union[int, None] = None

    def __repr__(self) -> str:  # pragma: no cover - debugging aid only
        if self.value is None:
            return f"Token({self.type.name})"
        return f"Token({self.type.name}, {self.value!r})"


# Characters that map directly onto a single-character token type.
_SINGLE_CHAR_TOKENS = {
    "+": TokenType.PLUS,
    "-": TokenType.MINUS,
    "*": TokenType.STAR,
    "/": TokenType.SLASH,
    "(": TokenType.LPAREN,
    ")": TokenType.RPAREN,
}


class TokenizerError(Exception):
    """Raised when the tokenizer encounters text it cannot make sense of."""


class Tokenizer:
    """Turns a raw source string into a list of :class:`Token` objects.

    The tokenizer is deliberately simple: it makes a single left to
    right pass over the input, skipping whitespace, recognising runs
    of digits as integer literals, and mapping the four operator
    characters and two parenthesis characters onto their token
    types. Anything else raises :class:`TokenizerError`.
    """

    def __init__(self, text: str) -> None:
        self._text = text
        self._pos = 0
        self._length = len(text)

    def _current_char(self) -> Union[str, None]:
        """Return the character under the cursor, or None at end of input."""
        if self._pos >= self._length:
            return None
        return self._text[self._pos]

    def _advance(self) -> None:
        """Move the cursor one character to the right."""
        self._pos += 1

    def _skip_whitespace(self) -> None:
        """Consume any run of spaces, tabs or newlines under the cursor."""
        while self._current_char() is not None and self._current_char().isspace():
            self._advance()

    def _read_integer(self) -> int:
        """Consume a contiguous run of digits and return it as an int."""
        start = self._pos
        while self._current_char() is not None and self._current_char().isdigit():
            self._advance()
        digits = self._text[start:self._pos]
        return int(digits)

    def tokenize(self) -> List[Token]:
        """Convert the whole input string into a list of tokens.

        The returned list always ends with a single ``EOF`` token,
        which lets the parser check for the end of input without
        special-casing ``None`` everywhere.
        """
        tokens: List[Token] = []
        while True:
            self._skip_whitespace()
            char = self._current_char()

            if char is None:
                tokens.append(Token(TokenType.EOF))
                break

            if char.isdigit():
                value = self._read_integer()
                tokens.append(Token(TokenType.INTEGER, value))
                continue

            if char in _SINGLE_CHAR_TOKENS:
                tokens.append(Token(_SINGLE_CHAR_TOKENS[char]))
                self._advance()
                continue

            raise TokenizerError(
                f"Unexpected character {char!r} at position {self._pos}"
            )

        return tokens


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Abstract syntax tree
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Num:
    """An integer literal, e.g. the ``42`` in ``42 + 1``."""

    value: int


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class UnaryOp:
    """A unary plus or minus applied to a single operand, e.g. ``-7``."""

    op: TokenType
    operand: "Node"


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class BinOp:
    """A binary operation with a left and right operand, e.g. ``3 + 4``."""

    op: TokenType
    left: "Node"
    right: "Node"


Node = Union[Num, UnaryOp, BinOp]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Parser
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


class ParseError(Exception):
    """Raised when the token stream does not match the expected grammar."""


class Parser:
    """A recursive descent parser for the arithmetic grammar described
    in the module docstring.

    Each grammar rule (``expression``, ``term``, ``factor``) is
    implemented as one method, and each method returns a small AST
    node built from :class:`Num`, :class:`UnaryOp` and
    :class:`BinOp`. Operator precedence falls straight out of the
    structure of the grammar: ``term`` is built from ``factor`` nodes
    connected by ``*``/``/``, and ``expression`` is built from
    ``term`` nodes connected by ``+``/``-``, so multiplication and
    division always bind tighter than addition and subtraction.
    """

    def __init__(self, tokens: List[Token]) -> None:
        self._tokens = tokens
        self._pos = 0

    def _current(self) -> Token:
        """Return the token currently under the cursor."""
        return self._tokens[self._pos]

    def _eat(self, expected_type: TokenType) -> Token:
        """Consume the current token if it matches, otherwise raise.

        Returns the consumed token so callers that need its value
        (only ``INTEGER`` tokens carry one) can use it directly.
        """
        token = self._current()
        if token.type is not expected_type:
            raise ParseError(
                f"Expected token {expected_type.name}, got {token.type.name}"
            )
        self._pos += 1
        return token

    def parse(self) -> Node:
        """Parse the full token stream and return the root AST node.

        Raises :class:`ParseError` if there are leftover tokens after
        a complete expression has been parsed, which catches errors
        such as a trailing stray operator or an unmatched closing
        parenthesis.
        """
        node = self._expression()
        self._eat(TokenType.EOF)
        return node

    def _expression(self) -> Node:
        """expression := term (("+" | "-") term)*"""
        node = self._term()
        while self._current().type in (TokenType.PLUS, TokenType.MINUS):
            op_token = self._current()
            self._eat(op_token.type)
            right = self._term()
            node = BinOp(op=op_token.type, left=node, right=right)
        return node

    def _term(self) -> Node:
        """term := factor (("*" | "/") factor)*"""
        node = self._factor()
        while self._current().type in (TokenType.STAR, TokenType.SLASH):
            op_token = self._current()
            self._eat(op_token.type)
            right = self._factor()
            node = BinOp(op=op_token.type, left=node, right=right)
        return node

    def _factor(self) -> Node:
        """factor := INTEGER | "(" expression ")" | ("+" | "-") factor"""
        token = self._current()

        if token.type is TokenType.INTEGER:
            self._eat(TokenType.INTEGER)
            assert token.value is not None
            return Num(token.value)

        if token.type is TokenType.LPAREN:
            self._eat(TokenType.LPAREN)
            node = self._expression()
            self._eat(TokenType.RPAREN)
            return node

        if token.type in (TokenType.PLUS, TokenType.MINUS):
            self._eat(token.type)
            operand = self._factor()
            return UnaryOp(op=token.type, operand=operand)

        raise ParseError(f"Unexpected token {token.type.name} in factor position")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Evaluator
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------


def evaluate_node(node: Node) -> Union[int, float]:
    """Recursively walk an AST produced by :class:`Parser` and compute
    its numeric value.

    Integers stay integers for as long as possible; only division
    (``/``) ever introduces a float, exactly as with Python's own
    arithmetic operators.
    """
    if isinstance(node, Num):
        return node.value

    if isinstance(node, UnaryOp):
        value = evaluate_node(node.operand)
        if node.op is TokenType.MINUS:
            return -value
        return value  # unary plus is a no-op

    if isinstance(node, BinOp):
        left = evaluate_node(node.left)
        right = evaluate_node(node.right)
        if node.op is TokenType.PLUS:
            return left + right
        if node.op is TokenType.MINUS:
            return left - right
        if node.op is TokenType.STAR:
            return left * right
        if node.op is TokenType.SLASH:
            return left / right
        raise ValueError(f"Unknown binary operator {node.op}")  # pragma: no cover

    raise TypeError(f"Unknown AST node type: {type(node)!r}")  # pragma: no cover


def evaluate(text: str) -> Union[int, float]:
    """Tokenize, parse and evaluate a single arithmetic expression.

    This is the convenience entry point most callers want: pass in a
    string such as ``"2 + 3 * (4 - 1)"`` and get back the numeric
    result, in this case ``11``.
    """
    tokens = Tokenizer(text).tokenize()
    tree = Parser(tokens).parse()
    return evaluate_node(tree)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Self-checks
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# A small set of assertions exercising tokenizing, parsing, operator
# precedence, parentheses, unary minus, whitespace handling and error
# reporting. These double as executable documentation of the module's
# behaviour.

assert evaluate("2 + 3 * 4") == 14
assert evaluate("(2 + 3) * 4") == 20
assert evaluate("10 - 2 - 3") == 5
assert evaluate("2 * (3 + (4 - 1) * 2)") == 18
assert evaluate("100 / 4 / 5") == 5.0
assert evaluate("-5 + 3") == -2
assert evaluate("-(3 + 4)") == -7
assert evaluate("2 + -3 * 4") == -10
assert evaluate("   12   +    8  ") == 20
assert evaluate("7") == 7
assert evaluate("1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5") == 15
assert evaluate("2 * 2 * 2 * 2") == 16

try:
    evaluate("2 +")
    assert False, "expected a ParseError for an incomplete expression"
except ParseError:
    pass

try:
    evaluate("(1 + 2")
    assert False, "expected a ParseError for an unmatched parenthesis"
except ParseError:
    pass

try:
    evaluate("2 & 3")
    assert False, "expected a TokenizerError for an unsupported character"
except TokenizerError:
    pass

text:
The London Underground began not as a single, planned system but as a set of competing private railway schemes built to relieve appalling road congestion in the world's largest city during the mid nineteenth century. The first section, the Metropolitan Railway, opened on 10 January 1863 between Paddington and Farringdon Street. It was built using the cut and cover method, in which a trench was dug along an existing road, brick tunnels were built inside it, and the road was then relaid on top. Steam locomotives hauled the original trains, and although this filled the tunnels with smoke and steam, ventilation shafts and open sections helped clear the air enough that the service proved immediately popular, carrying nearly 40,000 passengers on its opening day alone.

Success bred rapid expansion. The Metropolitan Railway extended west and north through the 1860s and 1870s, eventually reaching as far as Amersham and Chesham in the county of Buckinghamshire, a stretch that later gave rise to the term Metro-land, used to describe the new suburbs built along the line. A rival company, the Metropolitan District Railway, opened in 1868 and worked with the Metropolitan to complete an inner ring of track around central London, finished in 1884 and known today as the Circle line. Both companies used similar cut and cover construction and both suffered from smoke-filled stations, since steam engines remained the only practical form of traction until electric power became reliable enough for underground use.

A very different kind of underground railway appeared in 1890, when the City and South London Railway opened between King William Street in the City and Stockwell south of the river. Rather than digging a trench from the surface, engineers used a circular tunneling shield, a technique refined by Peter William Barlow and James Henry Greathead, to bore a narrow tube deep below the streets, avoiding the need to disturb buildings, sewers, and existing infrastructure above. Because steam locomotives could not operate safely in such confined tunnels, the line used electric traction from the outset, making it the world's first major electric underground railway and giving the network its enduring nickname, the Tube.

The years around 1900 brought a burst of new deep tube lines, financed in large part by the American transport magnate Charles Tyson Yerkes, who arrived in London after a controversial career building streetcar and elevated railway systems in Chicago. Yerkes consolidated several struggling and half-built tube schemes into the Underground Electric Railways Company of London, which opened the Bakerloo, Piccadilly, and part of what became the Northern line in quick succession between 1906 and 1907. His companies also electrified the existing District Railway and introduced a shared architectural style for stations, most visibly the distinctive ox-blood glazed tiles designed by the architect Leslie Green, many of which survive on station facades to this day.

Yerkes died in 1906, before most of his projects were finished, but the organisation he built survived and grew into the London Passenger Transport Board, formed in 1933 to unify the Underground, buses, and trams under a single public authority. This period is closely associated with Frank Pick, the managing director whose insistence on consistent design gave the network its familiar visual identity, including the red and blue roundel symbol and the modernist Johnston typeface still used across the system. In 1933 the Underground also adopted a radically simplified diagrammatic map designed by an electrical draughtsman named Harry Beck, who treated the network more like a circuit diagram than a geographically accurate map, spacing stations evenly and using only horizontal, vertical, and 45 degree lines. Passengers loved it immediately, and variations of Beck's design are still used by transit systems around the world.

During the Second World War many stations took on an unplanned second role as air raid shelters, with Londoners sleeping on platforms and in disused tunnels through the Blitz, sometimes in huge numbers organised with bunks, canteens, and even makeshift libraries. Some unfinished or little used sections were converted into aircraft factories or government offices, hidden from view beneath the ordinary business of running trains above them. After the war, several deep level shelters built specifically for wartime use were later opened to the public or repurposed for storage and telecommunications.

The decades after the war brought a period of relative stagnation, as investment favoured roads and the newly nationalised railways elsewhere, and only two entirely new lines were built in the second half of the twentieth century. The Victoria line, opened in stages between 1968 and 1971, was the first line built right across central London since the 1900s and introduced automatic train operation, in which trains ran under computer control with a driver present mainly to open and close doors and respond to emergencies. The Jubilee line followed in 1979, initially reusing existing tunnels before a major extension opened in 1999 to serve the redeveloped docklands area around Canary Wharf, built with unusually large stations designed to handle heavy future demand.

The twenty-first century Underground has focused less on building new lines and more on modernising what already exists, replacing worn out signalling, refurbishing stations, and extending step free access to a network that was, for the most part, designed and built more than a century before accessibility became a legal requirement. The most significant recent addition to London's rail network, the Elizabeth line, opened in 2022, and though technically operated separately from the Underground, it shares stations and ticketing with the older system and was built using the same tunneling expertise developed over more than a hundred and fifty years. Today the Underground carries around five million passenger journeys on an average weekday across eleven lines and more than two hundred and fifty stations, remaining both a practical necessity for the city and a piece of engineering history still visible in its Victorian brickwork, its ox-blood tiles, and the deceptively simple map that Harry Beck sketched out in his spare time nearly a century ago.

text:
French cuisine is often discussed in terms of its regions rather than as a single tradition, and nowhere is that more obvious than in the contrast between the rich, butter-and-cream cooking of the north and the olive-oil-driven cuisine of the Mediterranean south. In Normandy and Brittany, dishes lean on dairy, cider, and seafood, while in Provence, tomatoes, garlic, and herbes de Provence dominate dishes like ratatouille and the fish stew bouillabaisse, a Marseille speciality traditionally made with several kinds of Mediterranean fish and a saffron-scented broth, served with a garlicky rouille sauce spread on toasted bread. Further inland, the Périgord region of southwestern France is famous for foie gras and black truffles, ingredients that appear in everything from simple pan-seared preparations to elaborate terrines, while nearby Bordeaux lends its name to wine-based sauces built on reductions of the region's own red wine.

Bourgogne, or Burgundy, gave French cooking two of its most enduring dishes: boeuf bourguignon, beef slowly braised in red wine with mushrooms and pearl onions, and coq au vin, a similar treatment applied to chicken, both dishes born from the practical need to tenderize tougher cuts of meat over long, slow cooking. Alsace, on the German border, brings a different sensibility entirely, favouring choucroute garnie, a hearty dish of sauerkraut with sausages and cured pork, alongside crisp white wines like Riesling and Gewürztraminer. And no survey of French food would be complete without its desserts: crème brûlée, with its shattering caramelized sugar crust over silky custard, crème caramel, tarte Tatin, the upside-down caramelized apple tart said to have been invented by accident at a hotel in the Sologne, and the endless variety of pâtisserie found in nearly every French town, from mille-feuille to éclairs to the humble but perfect croissant.

Spanish cuisine shares some Mediterranean instincts with southern France but develops them very differently, shaped heavily by the country's Moorish history, its long Atlantic and Mediterranean coastlines, and strong regional identities. In Andalucía, in the deep south, gazpacho, a chilled soup of tomatoes, peppers, cucumber, and bread, offers relief from summer heat, while fried fish, pescaíto frito, reflects the region's coastal abundance. Jamón ibérico, cured ham from black Iberian pigs that forage on acorns in the dehesa woodlands, is treated with an almost ceremonial reverence, sliced thin by hand and served simply, often alongside manchego cheese and a glass of sherry from Jerez. Moving north and east into Cataluña, the cooking becomes more experimental, home to pan con tomate, bread rubbed with ripe tomato and olive oil, and to the roots of modern culinary techniques championed by chefs associated with the region's avant-garde restaurant scene.

The Basque Country, straddling the border with France, has its own distinct food culture built around pintxos, small snacks pinned with toothpicks onto slices of bread and served in bars across San Sebastián, alongside a strong tradition of seafood cookery and the lightly sparkling white wine txakoli. Paella, perhaps Spain's most internationally recognized dish, actually originates specifically from Valencia, traditionally made with rabbit, chicken, and green beans cooked with rice and saffron in a wide, shallow pan, though seafood versions have become far more common outside the region itself. Tortilla española, a thick omelette of eggs, potatoes, and onion, appears everywhere from tapas bars to home kitchens, a dish simple enough to make daily yet debated endlessly over whether onion belongs in it at all.

Portuguese cuisine, though often overshadowed internationally by its Spanish neighbour, has its own strong identity built around the Atlantic. Bacalhau, dried and salted cod, is so central to Portuguese cooking that it is said there are as many recipes for it as there are days in the year, prepared boiled, baked, fried, or shredded into dishes like bacalhau à brás, mixed with matchstick potatoes, eggs, and olives. Along the Algarve coast in the south, cataplana, a dish of clams, sausage, and vegetables cooked in a distinctive hinged copper pan of the same name, reflects the strong Moorish and Mediterranean influence on Portuguese coastal cooking. In the north, around Porto, the francesinha, a towering sandwich of cured meats and sausage smothered in melted cheese and a spiced tomato and beer sauce, represents a heartier, more indulgent tradition, often paired with the region's famous fortified wine or, more casually, a glass of the young, slightly effervescent vinho verde produced in the Minho region.

Portugal's sweets lean heavily on eggs and sugar, a legacy of convents that once produced pastries to use up egg yolks left over after using egg whites to starch clothing and clarify wine. The most famous result is the pastel de nata, a small custard tart with a flaky, blistered pastry shell, best eaten warm with a dusting of cinnamon, and closely associated with the Belém district of Lisbon, where the original recipe is still guarded as a closely held secret. Piri-piri, a fiery sauce made from small African bird's eye chillies brought back through Portugal's historic maritime trade routes, seasons grilled chicken across the country and has since spread internationally through Portuguese-influenced restaurants.

Taken together, these three cuisines show how geography, history, and trade shaped what ended up on the table: French cooking refined by regional wine and dairy traditions, Spanish cooking layered with Moorish spice routes and coastal abundance, and Portuguese cooking defined by its long relationship with the Atlantic Ocean and the trade networks it once commanded. Despite sharing a peninsula and, in places, a border, Spanish and Portuguese food remain distinctly their own, just as Provençal cooking bears little resemblance to the richer fare of Alsace or Bourgogne further north, a reminder that national cuisines are rarely single things at all.

The auction house at Greaves Fold smelled of hay dust, machine oil, and the particular damp-wool smell that seemed to follow every farmer through the door on a wet Tuesday in March. Ruth Calloway stood near the back wall, arms crossed over her coat, watching her father's old dresser get wheeled onto the rostrum with a squeak of castors that made her wince.

"Lot forty-two," called the auctioneer, a broad man named Pemberton whose voice carried to the rafters without any apparent effort. "Oak dresser, three drawers, a bit of woodworm in the back panel if you look close, but a good solid piece. Who'll start me at twenty?"

Nobody moved. Ada Fenwick, seated in her usual spot on the second row with a flask of tea balanced on her knee (a flask she'd owned, by all accounts, longer than most marriages in the village lasted), tutted loud enough for half the room to hear. "Twenty pounds for that? My mother used to say, 'A good dresser outlives three husbands and never once complains,' and she wasn't wrong about that one."

"Your mother," Pemberton said without missing a beat, "wasn't bidding against half of Cumbria for reclaimed oak, Ada. Now who'll start me at twenty? Fifteen, then. Someone save me the embarrassment!"

A hand went up near the front, Callum Whitfield, a dealer Ruth recognised from the market in town, the sort of man who bought things not because he wanted them but because he knew someone who would. "Fifteen," he said, not even looking up from his phone.

"Fifteen I have. Twenty? Twenty, thank you, twenty-five, Callum? Don't tell me you're done already."

"I'm thinking," Callum said, which made Ada snort into her tea.

Ruth's chest tightened. It wasn't much, this dresser, not really, just an old thing with a wobbly leg and a drawer that stuck in damp weather, but it had sat in her parents' kitchen for as long as she could remember, and now it was lot forty-two, going for whatever a room full of strangers decided it was worth on a Tuesday morning.

"You alright, love?" Ada asked, twisting round in her seat, flask still balanced with the practiced ease of someone who had spent decades not spilling tea at auctions.

"I'm fine," Ruth said, which wasn't strictly true, but there wasn't a tidy way to explain that watching your childhood get auctioned off in ten-pound increments does something strange to a person.

"Twenty-five I have from the front," Pemberton continued. "Thirty? Come on, it's Tuesday, you've nothing better to spend it on, thirty, thank you. Thirty-five?"

Callum raised two fingers without looking up.

"Forty, is it? Or are we stopping at thirty-five?"

"Forty," Callum said, finally glancing toward the piece as though remembering it existed as an object and not just a number.

Ada leaned toward Ruth, dropping her voice to what she clearly believed was a whisper but which carried perfectly well to the next three rows. "He'll go to sixty. Watch. He always goes to sixty and stops, like it's a rule he's set himself."

"Is that true?" Ruth asked.

"It's been true every Tuesday for eleven years," Ada said, with the flat certainty of someone who had clearly kept count.

The bidding crept upward: forty-five, fifty, fifty-five; Pemberton's voice never rising, never dropping, just rolling steadily forward like a man walking uphill at a pace he could keep all day. At sixty, right on schedule, Callum's hand stayed in his lap.

"Sixty I have. Sixty, any advance on sixty? Going once, going—"

"Sixty-five," said Ada, setting her flask down with a decisiveness that startled even her.

The whole row turned to look at her. Pemberton, to his credit, barely blinked. "Sixty-five from Ada Fenwick, who I don't believe has bid on a single lot in eleven years."

"There's a first time for everything," Ada said, chin up. "That dresser's near enough the twin of the one my mother had, and I always regretted letting her sister take it when Mam passed. I'm not letting this one go to a man who'll have it in a shop window by Thursday with the price tripled."

Callum's hand twitched, hovered, and then rose again, more out of professional reflex than conviction. "Seventy."

"Seventy-five," Ada shot back, not even waiting for Pemberton to ask.

"He's off his own rule now," Pemberton said to the room at large, clearly enjoying himself. "Eleven years, gone, just like that."

Ruth let out a breath that was almost a laugh, the tightness in her chest loosening slightly for the first time all morning. "Ada, you don't have to—"

"I know I don't have to," Ada said, not looking away from Callum. "I want to. There's a difference, and I'll thank you to let an old woman have her moment."

The bidding went on, eighty, eighty-five, Callum's jaw set in the particular way of a man who has decided, somewhere around lot forty-two on a wet Tuesday, that this has stopped being about the dresser and started being about something else entirely, until he finally shook his head and let his hand fall still at ninety.

"Ninety-five, going once, going twice," Pemberton called, the gavel already lifting, "sold, for ninety-five pounds, to Ada Fenwick, who has apparently been sitting on a bidding habit for eleven years and chose today, of all days, to unleash it!"

A ripple of laughter went round the room. Callum, to his credit, laughed too, shaking his head at his own phone as though it had somehow been responsible for talking him out of it.

Ruth watched two men in overalls carry the dresser toward the loading bay, its familiar wobble visible even in the way they held it, careful of the leg that had never quite sat right. It felt strange, she thought, that something could stop being hers in the space of ninety seconds and a few dozen raised hands, and stranger still that she felt, on balance, alright about it, especially now.

"Ninety-five pounds," Ada said, gathering her flask and her coat with the satisfied air of someone whose morning had gone exactly as entertainingly as she'd hoped, "and it's going two streets from where it started, to a woman who'll actually put something in every one of those drawers. Your mother would've called that a fair trade, I think, whatever she said about giving things away."

"She would have," Ruth agreed, and found, a little to her own surprise, that she was smiling.

text:
For most of the age of sail, navigators could determine their latitude, their position north or south of the equator, with reasonable confidence by measuring the angle of the sun at noon or of the pole star at night, tools and calculations well understood since antiquity. Longitude, position east or west, offered no such straightforward solution, and this gap between what sailors could and could not measure caused shipwrecks, lost cargo, and thousands of deaths throughout the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries as vessels missed their intended landfalls or ran aground on coastlines they believed to be safely distant.

The underlying problem was fundamentally one of time rather than geometry. Because the earth rotates a full 360 degrees in 24 hours, each hour of difference between local time aboard ship and the time at a known reference point, such as the home port, corresponds to exactly 15 degrees of longitude. A navigator who could compare the ship's local time, easily found by observing when the sun reached its highest point, against the time back home would be able to calculate exactly how far east or west the ship had travelled. The difficulty was keeping accurate time at home while at sea, since no clock of the period could survive the temperature swings, humidity, and constant motion of an ocean voyage without drifting wildly off true time within days.

Several European governments recognised the severity of the problem and offered substantial prizes for a workable solution. Spain and the Netherlands made early attempts at incentivising research in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, but the most consequential prize came from the British government, which passed the Longitude Act in 1714 following a series of naval disasters, most notoriously the wrecking of four ships of Sir Cloudesley Shovell's fleet on the Isles of Scilly in 1707, an incident that killed close to two thousand sailors and was widely, if not entirely fairly, blamed on a failure to determine position accurately. The Act established a Board of Longitude and offered a reward of up to twenty thousand pounds, an enormous sum at the time, for any method capable of determining longitude at sea to within specified degrees of accuracy.

Two broad approaches competed for the prize over the following decades. The first, favoured by most astronomers of the period, relied on observing predictable celestial events, most importantly the position of the moon relative to the stars, a method known as the lunar distance technique. By comparing the observed position of the moon against tables calculated in advance for a known location, typically the Royal Observatory at Greenwich, a skilled navigator could work out the time at that reference point and therefore the ship's longitude. The method worked, but it demanded difficult sextant observations, lengthy calculations that could take hours to complete by hand, and clear skies, none of which were reliably available aboard a rolling ship in bad weather. Nevil Maskelyne, who became Astronomer Royal in 1765, championed this approach and published the Nautical Almanac from 1767 onward, providing pre-calculated lunar distance tables that made the method far more practical for ordinary navigators to use.

The second approach, championed almost single-handedly by a self-taught Yorkshire carpenter and clockmaker named John Harrison, aimed to solve the problem mechanically rather than astronomically: build a clock accurate and robust enough to keep the home port's time reliably throughout a long ocean voyage, regardless of temperature changes, humidity, or the ship's motion. Harrison began work on the problem in the 1730s and spent the better part of four decades refining a series of increasingly sophisticated timekeepers. His first attempt, H1, completed in 1735, was a large and heavy machine built from wood and brass that used counterbalanced weights to compensate for the ship's rolling motion, and it performed well enough on a sea trial to encourage further funding from the Board of Longitude. Harrison continued refining his designs through H2 and H3, each addressing weaknesses discovered in the previous version, before making a crucial conceptual shift toward a much smaller and more portable design.

His fourth attempt, H4, completed in 1759, looked almost nothing like its predecessors: rather than a large mechanism, it resembled an oversized pocket watch, only about thirteen centimetres across, using a fast-beating balance wheel and a novel temperature-compensation mechanism to maintain accuracy despite changing conditions. On a trial voyage to Jamaica in 1761 and 1762, H4 lost only about five seconds over an eighty-one day voyage, an extraordinary result that comfortably exceeded the accuracy required for the full prize. Despite this success, the Board of Longitude, dominated by astronomers who favoured the lunar distance method and were reluctant to accept that a single craftsman working largely alone had solved a problem that had defeated the finest scientific minds in Europe, resisted awarding Harrison the full prize for years, demanding repeated trials, duplicate copies of his mechanism, and eventually direct intervention from King George III before Harrison received a substantial payment in 1773, though he was never formally awarded the prize outright.

Harrison's design proved that a marine chronometer was not only possible but practical, and once his methods became known, other clockmakers, particularly Larcum Kendall, who built a close copy known as K1, refined and eventually mass-produced chronometers based on similar principles. Captain James Cook carried a Kendall chronometer on his second voyage of exploration in the 1770s and praised it enthusiastically in his journals, helping cement the chronometer's reputation among working navigators. Through the late eighteenth and early nineteenth centuries, prices fell as production methods improved, and by the mid nineteenth century most ocean-going vessels carried at least one chronometer as standard equipment, checked periodically against observatory time whenever a ship called at a major port. The lunar distance method persisted alongside chronometers for decades, valued as a reliable backup that required no delicate mechanism, but the marine chronometer had effectively settled the longitude problem, transforming ocean navigation from an exercise in educated guesswork into a matter of precise, repeatable calculation, and the story of its development, particularly Harrison's long struggle against an unsympathetic scientific establishment, remains one of the most celebrated episodes in the history of navigation and horology alike.

text:
The Panama Canal's system of locks was engineered to lift ships over the isthmus's central highlands rather than attempt an impossibly deep sea-level cut through solid rock. When the canal opened in 1914, after French efforts under Ferdinand de Lesseps had collapsed in the 1880s amid disease and financial ruin, American engineers led by John Stevens and George Goethals adopted a lock-based design instead. Ships travelling from the Atlantic pass through the three-step Gatun Locks, which raise them 26 metres to the level of Gatun Lake, an artificial reservoir created by damming the Chagres River. Vessels then cross the lake and the Culebra Cut, a channel blasted through the continental divide, before descending through the Pedro Miguel and Miraflores Locks on the Pacific side.

Each lock chamber works on a simple principle of gravity-fed water transfer. Enormous valves open to let water flow from a higher chamber, or from the adjoining lake, into a lower one, raising or lowering the ship enclosed within massive concrete walls. No pumps are required for this movement, since the entire system relies on gravity alone; only the machinery that opens and closes the miter gates and valves needs power. Electric locomotives, known as mules, run on tracks along the lock walls and use cables to keep ships centred as they pass through the narrow chambers, since the vessels move under their own power but cannot steer precisely enough in such tight confines.

For nearly a century the original locks, each 33.5 metres wide, effectively capped the size of ship that could use the canal, a limit shipbuilders came to call Panamax. Growing global trade and ever larger container ships eventually made this constraint a serious bottleneck. A major expansion project, completed in 2016, added a third, wider lane of locks alongside the originals. These new locks use rolling gates instead of miter gates and incorporate water-saving basins that reuse roughly sixty percent of the water in each transit, reducing the enormous draw on Gatun Lake's freshwater supply. The expanded canal now accommodates Neopanamax vessels carrying far more cargo than the original locks ever could, keeping this hundred-year-old feat of engineering central to world shipping.

text:
Okay so it's officially been a year since I talked my partner into letting me put a beehive in the back corner of the garden, and I have THOUGHTS. Nobody tells you how much of beekeeping is just standing there in a slightly too-hot suit, sweating, staring at frames like you understand what you're looking at. Spoiler: for the first three months I absolutely did not.

I started with a single nucleus colony in April, five frames of bees and a queen I named Beyoncé because I figured if I was going to be nervous around fifty thousand insects I might as well be nervous around royalty. The first inspection was a disaster. I dropped a frame (thankfully into the hive, not onto the grass), got stung twice through my glove because apparently gardening gloves are not the flex I thought they were, and spent the rest of the day convinced I'd doomed the whole colony. They were fine. They did not care about my feelings at all, which honestly set the tone for the whole year.

Summer was the good bit. Watching them come back loaded with pollen, orange and yellow and this weird grey-blue from something in next door's garden, never stopped being satisfying. I got genuinely obsessed with figuring out what they were foraging on. There's a real detective-work side to this that nobody warns you about. By July the colony had built up enough that I added a second box, and by August I actually got a small harvest, about nine kilos, which felt like an insane amount of effort for what amounted to a few jars of honey, and also somehow completely worth it.

Autumn brought the varroa mite panic, which every beekeeping forum on earth had already warned me about and I still underestimated. Treated late, worried a lot, learned more about mite counts than I ever expected to know about anything. Winter was mostly anxious silence, tapping the side of the hive on mild days just to hear that reassuring hum and prove to myself they hadn't all quietly died while I wasn't looking.

They made it through. The cluster's smaller than I'd like going into spring, but they're alive, Beyoncé is apparently still queening, and I've already ordered a second hive for this year because apparently one wasn't enough chaos. Ask me again in twelve months whether that was a good idea.

text:
A B-tree index speeds up database lookups by organizing keys into a balanced, multi-way tree structure that keeps the number of disk reads needed to find a row small, even as a table grows into the millions of rows. Unlike a binary tree, where each node has at most two children, a B-tree node typically holds many keys and many children, often hundreds, depending on the page size the database engine uses to read data from disk. This wide branching factor is the whole point: because each node can be packed with so many keys, the tree stays shallow. A table with millions of rows might only need a tree three or four levels deep, meaning a lookup that would otherwise require scanning the entire table instead touches only three or four pages.

When you query a column with a B-tree index, the engine starts at the root node and compares your search value against the keys stored there to decide which child pointer to follow. It repeats this comparison at each level, narrowing the range of possible matches at every step, until it reaches a leaf node containing the actual row pointers or, in the case of a clustered index, the row data itself. Because internal nodes only store keys and pointers rather than full rows, they are small enough that entire levels, or even the whole upper portion of the tree, can be cached in memory, making repeated lookups very fast.

B-trees also keep themselves balanced automatically as data is inserted or deleted. When a node fills up and a new key needs to be inserted, the node splits into two and a key is pushed up to the parent; if that causes the parent to overflow, the split cascades upward, occasionally growing the tree by one level at the root. Deletions work in reverse, merging or borrowing keys from sibling nodes to keep every node reasonably full. This self-balancing behaviour guarantees that lookup, insertion, and deletion all cost roughly the same, predictable amount of work no matter how the data was inserted, which is why B-trees remain the default index structure in most relational databases.

The other major benefit is that B-trees preserve key order, so they support not just exact-match lookups but range queries, sorting, and prefix searches efficiently, which is exactly the kind of query pattern that shows up constantly in real applications, from filtering by date range to paginating results.

1. **Audit your current data.** Export every issue, comment, attachment, and custom field from the old tracker before touching anything else, and note which fields your team actually uses versus what has sat empty for years.
2. **Map fields between systems.** Match statuses, priorities, and issue types in the old tool to their nearest equivalent in the new one, and decide upfront where there's no clean match.
3. **Choose a cutover date.** Freeze new issue creation in the old tracker at a fixed time so nothing gets created or updated mid-migration and lost in the gap.
4. **Run a small pilot migration.** Move one project or a sample of fifty issues first, then have the team check the results before committing to the full migration.
5. **Preserve issue history.** Confirm whether comments, status changes, and timestamps carry over, since losing this context is the most common regret teams report afterward.
6. **Decide what not to migrate.** Archive or export closed issues older than a set cutoff instead of dragging years of stale tickets into the new system.
7. **Set up workflows first.** Build out statuses, transitions, and automation rules in the new tracker before importing data, so issues land in a structure that already works.
8. **Update integrations.** Reconnect version control, CI pipelines, chat notifications, and any other tools that referenced the old tracker's webhooks or API.
9. **Reassign ownership.** Check that assignees, watchers, and reporters map correctly to real user accounts in the new system rather than defaulting to a generic import user.
10. **Communicate the change early.** Give the team advance notice, a short how-to guide, and a clear date so nobody is caught mid-sprint with an unfamiliar tool.
11. **Keep the old tracker read-only.** Don't delete or cancel the old subscription immediately; keep it accessible in read-only mode for a few months in case something was missed.
12. **Review after two weeks.** Gather feedback once the team has actually used the new tracker day to day, and fix workflow friction while it's still fresh rather than letting it calcify.

"""A small least-recently-used (LRU) cache implementation.

This module provides a single class, LRUCache, backed by a dictionary
for O(1) lookups and a doubly linked list for O(1) reordering and
eviction of the least recently used entry.
"""


class _Node:
    """A single doubly linked list node holding a key/value pair."""

    __slots__ = ("key", "value", "prev", "next")

    def __init__(self, key=None, value=None):
        self.key = key
        self.value = value
        self.prev = None
        self.next = None


class LRUCache:
    """A fixed-capacity cache that evicts the least recently used item.

    Both get and put run in O(1) time. Recency is tracked with a
    doubly linked list: the most recently used item sits right after
    the head sentinel, and the least recently used item sits right
    before the tail sentinel.
    """

    def __init__(self, capacity):
        if capacity <= 0:
            raise ValueError("capacity must be a positive integer")

        self.capacity = capacity
        self._map = {}

        # Sentinel nodes remove the need for special-casing empty lists.
        self._head = _Node()
        self._tail = _Node()
        self._head.next = self._tail
        self._tail.prev = self._head

    def get(self, key):
        """Return the value for key, or None if key is not present.

        A successful lookup marks the entry as most recently used.
        """
        node = self._map.get(key)
        if node is None:
            return None

        self._move_to_front(node)
        return node.value

    def put(self, key, value):
        """Insert or update key with value, evicting if over capacity."""
        existing = self._map.get(key)

        if existing is not None:
            existing.value = value
            self._move_to_front(existing)
            return

        if len(self._map) >= self.capacity:
            self._evict_least_recently_used()

        node = _Node(key, value)
        self._map[key] = node
        self._insert_at_front(node)

    def _insert_at_front(self, node):
        # Splice node in right after the head sentinel.
        first = self._head.next
        node.prev = self._head
        node.next = first
        self._head.next = node
        first.prev = node

    def _remove(self, node):
        # Unlink node from wherever it currently sits.
        node.prev.next = node.next
        node.next.prev = node.prev

    def _move_to_front(self, node):
        self._remove(node)
        self._insert_at_front(node)

    def _evict_least_recently_used(self):
        # The entry just before the tail sentinel is the LRU item.
        lru = self._tail.prev
        self._remove(lru)
        del self._map[lru.key]

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self._map)

    def __contains__(self, key):
        return key in self._map

text:
The modern shipping container grew out of a fairly simple problem: loading and unloading cargo ship by ship, crate by crate, box by box, was slow, expensive, and prone to damage and theft. Through the first half of the twentieth century, break bulk cargo was hauled aboard piece by piece using nets and pallets, a process that could keep a ship tied up in port for a week or more while dockworkers manually stacked thousands of individual items into the hold.

The person most associated with solving this problem is Malcom McLean, an American trucking entrepreneur rather than a shipping man by background. McLean's insight, developed through the 1950s, was that instead of unloading a truck's cargo piece by piece onto a ship, the entire truck trailer body, minus its wheels, could be lifted as a single sealed unit and set directly into the hold. In 1956 his converted tanker ship, the Ideal X, carried fifty-eight of these standardized metal boxes from Newark to Houston, marking the first commercial container voyage of its kind.

What made the idea take off was not just the container itself but the standardization that followed. Competing shipping lines, railroads, and truck operators initially used incompatible box sizes and corner fittings, which limited how easily containers could move between different modes of transport. Through the 1960s the International Organization for Standardization worked with industry groups to agree on fixed container dimensions, most notably the twenty-foot and forty-foot lengths still used today, along with standardized corner castings that let cranes, ships, trucks, and trains all handle the same box without modification.

Ports had to change just as much as the boxes did. Traditional finger piers built for break bulk cargo gave way to large container terminals with vast paved yards, gantry cranes, and rail access, since a container port needed space to stack thousands of boxes rather than warehouse space for loose goods. Cities like Rotterdam, Singapore, and later Shanghai built their economic importance partly on early and aggressive investment in this new kind of infrastructure.

The economic effect was enormous. Loading costs per ton dropped by well over ninety percent within a couple of decades, and turnaround times in port fell from days to hours. Combined with jet air travel and later digital communication, the standardized container is often credited as one of the quiet engines behind the huge growth in global trade during the second half of the twentieth century, letting manufacturers place factories far from their end markets and still ship goods cheaply and reliably around the world.

text:
Vienna and Prague sit at the heart of two overlapping musical traditions, one Austro-German and one Czech, that shaped much of what we now call classical music. Vienna's claim is the more famous: Haydn, Mozart, Beethoven, and later Brahms all worked in the city, drawn by imperial patronage and a dense concentration of aristocratic households eager to fund private orchestras and chamber ensembles. The Vienna Philharmonic, founded in 1842, still performs in the Musikverein's gilded Golden Hall, an auditorium whose acoustics are frequently cited as among the finest in the world. Later, Vienna became the unlikely birthplace of a very different tradition when Arnold Schönberg developed twelve-tone technique in the early twentieth century, abandoning conventional tonality altogether and influencing generations of composers who followed his lead, including his students Alban Berg and Anton Webern.

Prague's musical identity grew more explicitly nationalist. Bedřich Smetana, often considered the father of Czech classical music, composed his cycle of symphonic poems Má vlast as a tribute to the Bohemian landscape and history, with its famous movement Vltava tracing the course of the river through the countryside and into Prague itself. Antonín Dvořák, who studied under Smetana's influence, brought Czech folk idioms into symphonic and chamber forms with enormous international success, later spending several years in the United States, where he drew on African American spirituals and Native American melodies for his New World Symphony before returning home. Leoš Janáček took Czech nationalism somewhere stranger and more modern, building his operatic style directly on the rhythms and inflections of spoken Czech speech, producing works like Jenůfa and The Cunning Little Vixen that sound like almost nothing else from the period.

The two cities were never entirely separate. Mozart considered Prague his most appreciative audience and premiered Don Giovanni there in 1787 rather than in Vienna, reportedly telling friends that Praguers understood him better than his own countrymen did. French composers occasionally entered this Central European conversation too; Gabriel Fauré never lived in either city, but his harmonic language influenced how later Czech and Austrian composers thought about colour and ambiguity within otherwise traditional forms. Together, Vienna's institutional grandeur and Prague's folk-rooted intensity produced two of the richest and most distinct classical music cultures in Europe, still audible in concert halls and opera houses across both cities today.

text:
The waiting room smelled of wet wool and old radiators. Frances sat closest to the fire, her suitcase balanced on her knees like a shield, while Tomas paced by the window, checking his watch every few minutes as though that might hurry the train along.

"You'll wear a groove in the floor," said the third occupant, an elderly man named Griggs who'd claimed the bench by the door an hour earlier and hadn't moved since. "Sit down. It's not coming any faster for your pacing."

Tomas didn't sit. "My sister's expecting me at six. If I miss this one, I don't get another until—" He stopped mid-sentence, glancing at the departures board as if it might have changed in the last thirty seconds.

"Until tomorrow," Frances finished for him, not unkindly. "We know. You've said it four times."

Griggs chuckled, a dry sound like paper rustling. "Reminds me of my own father. Man never sat still in a waiting room in his life. Used to say, 'A watched train's like a watched pot, it takes its sweet time out of spite.'" He shook his head. "Course, he also missed his own brother's wedding by pacing straight past the platform, so take that wisdom as you like."

Frances laughed despite herself, and even Tomas's shoulders eased a fraction. "That's oddly comforting," he admitted, finally lowering himself onto the bench beside her (though he kept his coat buttoned, ready to bolt the moment the tannoy crackled).

"It wasn't meant to be comforting," Griggs said. "It was meant to be true. There's a difference, though not always a large one."

A distant rumble rolled through the walls, and all three of them straightened at once, Tomas's suitcase already half off his lap.

"That'll be it," Frances said, standing.

"Or the 4:15 to somewhere else entirely," Griggs muttered, not moving from his bench in the slightest. "I've learned not to trust the first sound. Wait for the second one, the one that actually stops."

They waited. The second rumble came, closer this time, and the tannoy finally crackled to life overhead. Tomas was already at the door before the announcement finished, calling back over his shoulder, "Thank you, both of you, really," in a voice that cracked slightly with relief.

Griggs didn't look up from his newspaper. "Go on then. Don't miss your sister's dinner on my account."

Frances lingered a moment longer, watching the old man settle back into his corner of the room as though he intended to wait there forever.

text:
When the Panama Canal opened to traffic in August 1914, its solution to crossing the isthmus was not to dig a sea-level channel straight through the mountainous spine of Panama, an approach the French had already tried and abandoned at enormous human cost in the 1880s, but to lift ships bodily over the high ground using a staircase of locks. The American engineering team that took over the project in 1904, led first by John Stevens and later by George Goethals, judged a lock canal far more achievable than the sea-level design de Lesseps had favoured, and also far more resistant to the landslides that had plagued excavation work in the Culebra Cut.

Ships entering from the Caribbean side climb through the three chambers of the Gatun Locks, rising a combined 26 metres until they reach Gatun Lake, a vast reservoir formed by damming the Chagres River specifically to supply the canal with water and to shorten the distance vessels needed to travel under lock power alone. After crossing the lake and threading through the Culebra Cut, ships descend again through the Pedro Miguel Lock and then the two-stage Miraflores Locks before reaching the Pacific.

The locks themselves move ships using nothing but gravity. Water flows downhill from the lake through large culverts into a lock chamber, raising the vessel inside to match the level of the next chamber up, or drains out again to lower it, all without a single pump. Massive steel miter gates, some of the largest moving structures ever built when the canal opened, seal each chamber, while small electric locomotives called mules run along tracks on the lock walls, using cables to keep the ship centred since it cannot manoeuvre itself precisely in such a narrow space.

For most of the canal's history, the width of these original chambers, just over 33 metres, effectively defined the maximum size of oceangoing vessel, a category shipbuilders still refer to as Panamax. As container ships grew far beyond that limit through the late twentieth century, Panama undertook a second major construction effort, completing a new, wider set of locks in 2016 that use sliding rather than miter gates and recycle a large share of their water through adjacent basins. A century after its first transit, the canal remains one of the few pieces of infrastructure whose basic engineering principle, water moving ships uphill and down by gravity alone, has changed remarkably little.

text: Sedimentary rock forms when particles of sand, silt, clay, or organic debris settle out of water, ice, or wind and accumulate in layers. As more material piles on top, the growing weight compresses the lower layers, squeezing out water and pressing grains together. Groundwater carrying dissolved minerals, often calcite or silica, seeps through the remaining gaps and precipitates, cementing the grains into solid rock, a process called lithification. This usually happens over thousands or millions of years in riverbeds, deltas, lake bottoms, and ocean floors, producing rocks such as sandstone, shale, and limestone, which frequently preserve fossils and layering.

text: A hash collision happens when two different inputs produce the same output from a hash function. Since hash functions map an effectively unbounded input space onto a fixed-size output space, collisions are mathematically unavoidable, though a good function makes them rare and unpredictable. In hash tables, collisions mean two keys land in the same bucket, so you need a resolution strategy like chaining or open addressing. In cryptographic contexts, collisions are more serious, since an attacker who can deliberately produce two inputs with the same hash can forge signatures or tamper with data undetected.

def merge_intervals(intervals):
    """Merge a list of overlapping integer intervals.

    Each interval is a sequence of two integers (start, end) with
    start <= end. Returns a new list of merged, non-overlapping
    intervals sorted by start value.
    """
    if not intervals:
        return []

    sorted_intervals = sorted(intervals, key=lambda pair: pair[0])
    merged = [list(sorted_intervals[0])]

    for start, end in sorted_intervals[1:]:
        last = merged[-1]
        if start <= last[1]:
            last[1] = max(last[1], end)
        else:
            merged.append([start, end])

    return [tuple(interval) for interval in merged]

CHAPTER I.
Down the Rabbit-Hole


Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the
bank, and of having nothing to do: once or twice she had peeped into
the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or
conversations in it, “and what is the use of a book,” thought Alice
“without pictures or conversations?”

So she was considering in her own mind (as well as she could, for the
hot day made her feel very sleepy and stupid), whether the pleasure of
making a daisy-chain would be worth the trouble of getting up and
picking the daisies, when suddenly a White Rabbit with pink eyes ran
close by her.

There was nothing so _very_ remarkable in that; nor did Alice think it
so _very_ much out of the way to hear the Rabbit say to itself, “Oh
dear! Oh dear! I shall be late!” (when she thought it over afterwards,
it occurred to her that she ought to have wondered at this, but at the
time it all seemed quite natural); but when the Rabbit actually _took a
watch out of its waistcoat-pocket_, and looked at it, and then hurried
on, Alice started to her feet, for it flashed across her mind that she
had never before seen a rabbit with either a waistcoat-pocket, or a
watch to take out of it, and burning with curiosity, she ran across the
field after it, and fortunately was just in time to see it pop down a
large rabbit-hole under the hedge.

In another moment down went Alice after it, never once considering how
in the world she was to get out again.

The rabbit-hole went straight on like a tunnel for some way, and then
dipped suddenly down, so suddenly that Alice had not a moment to think
about stopping herself before she found herself falling down a very
deep well.

Either the well was very deep, or she fell very slowly, for she had
plenty of time as she went down to look about her and to wonder what
was going to happen next. First, she tried to look down and make out
what she was coming to, but it was too dark to see anything; then she
looked at the sides of the well, and noticed that they were filled with
cupboards and book-shelves; here and there she saw maps and pictures
hung upon pegs. She took down a jar from one of the shelves as she
passed; it was labelled “ORANGE MARMALADE”, but to her great
disappointment it was empty: she did not like to drop the jar for fear
of killing somebody underneath, so managed to put it into one of the
cupboards as she fell past it.

“Well!” thought Alice to herself, “after such a fall as this, I shall
think nothing of tumbling down stairs! How brave they’ll all think me
at home! Why, I wouldn’t say anything about it, even if I fell off the
top of the house!” (Which was very likely true.)

Down, down, down. Would the fall _never_ come to an end? “I wonder how
many miles I’ve fallen by this time?” she said aloud. “I must be
getting somewhere near the centre of the earth. Let me see: that would
be four thousand miles down, I think—” (for, you see, Alice had learnt
several things of this sort in her lessons in the schoolroom, and
though this was not a _very_ good opportunity for showing off her
knowledge, as there was no one to listen to her, still it was good
practice to say it over) “—yes, that’s about the right distance—but
then I wonder what Latitude or Longitude I’ve got to?” (Alice had no
idea what Latitude was, or Longitude either, but thought they were nice
grand words to say.)

Presently she began again. “I wonder if I shall fall right _through_
the earth! How funny it’ll seem to come out among the people that walk
with their heads downward! The Antipathies, I think—” (she was rather
glad there _was_ no one listening, this time, as it didn’t sound at all
the right word) “—but I shall have to ask them what the name of the
country is, you know. Please, Ma’am, is this New Zealand or Australia?”
(and she tried to curtsey as she spoke—fancy _curtseying_ as you’re
falling through the air! Do you think you could manage it?) “And what
an ignorant little girl she’ll think me for asking! No, it’ll never do
to ask: perhaps I shall see it written up somewhere.”

Down, down, down. There was nothing else to do, so Alice soon began
talking again. “Dinah’ll miss me very much to-night, I should think!”
(Dinah was the cat.) “I hope they’ll remember her saucer of milk at
tea-time. Dinah my dear! I wish you were down here with me! There are
no mice in the air, I’m afraid, but you might catch a bat, and that’s
very like a mouse, you know. But do cats eat bats, I wonder?” And here
Alice began to get rather sleepy, and went on saying to herself, in a
dreamy sort of way, “Do cats eat bats? Do cats eat bats?” and
sometimes, “Do bats eat cats?” for, you see, as she couldn’t answer
either question, it didn’t much matter which way she put it. She felt
that she was dozing off, and had just begun to dream that she was
walking hand in hand with Dinah, and saying to her very earnestly,
“Now, Dinah, tell me the truth: did you ever eat a bat?” when suddenly,
thump! thump! down she came upon a heap of sticks and dry leaves, and
the fall was over.

Alice was not a bit hurt, and she jumped up on to her feet in a moment:
she looked up, but it was all dark overhead; before her was another
long passage, and the White Rabbit was still in sight, hurrying down
it. There was not a moment to be lost: away went Alice like the wind,
and was just in time to hear it say, as it turned a corner, “Oh my ears
and whiskers, how late it’s getting!” She was close behind it when she
turned the corner, but the Rabbit was no longer to be seen: she found
herself in a long, low hall, which was lit up by a row of lamps hanging
from the roof.

There were doors all round the hall, but they were all locked; and when
Alice had been all the way down one side and up the other, trying every
door, she walked sadly down the middle, wondering how she was ever to
get out again.

Suddenly she came upon a little three-legged table, all made of solid
glass; there was nothing on it except a tiny golden key, and Alice’s
first thought was that it might belong to one of the doors of the hall;
but, alas! either the locks were too large, or the key was too small,
but at any rate it would not open any of them. However, on the second
time round, she came upon a low curtain she had not noticed before, and
behind it was a little door about fifteen inches high: she tried the
little golden key in the lock, and to her great delight it fitted!

Alice opened the door and found that it led into a small passage, not
much larger than a rat-hole: she knelt down and looked along the
passage into the loveliest garden you ever saw. How she longed to get
out of that dark hall, and wander about among those beds of bright
flowers and those cool fountains, but she could not even get her head
through the doorway; “and even if my head would go through,” thought
poor Alice, “it would be of very little use without my shoulders. Oh,
how I wish I could shut up like a telescope! I think I could, if I only
knew how to begin.” For, you see, so many out-of-the-way things had
happened lately, that Alice had begun to think that very few things
indeed were really impossible.

There seemed to be no use in waiting by the little door, so she went
back to the table, half hoping she might find another key on it, or at
any rate a book of rules for shutting people up like telescopes: this
time she found a little bottle on it, (“which certainly was not here
before,” said Alice,) and round the neck of the bottle was a paper
label, with the words “DRINK ME,” beautifully printed on it in large
letters.

It was all very well to say “Drink me,” but the wise little Alice was
not going to do _that_ in a hurry. “No, I’ll look first,” she said,
“and see whether it’s marked ‘_poison_’ or not”; for she had read
several nice little histories about children who had got burnt, and
eaten up by wild beasts and other unpleasant things, all because they
_would_ not remember the simple rules their friends had taught them:
such as, that a red-hot poker will burn you if you hold it too long;
and that if you cut your finger _very_ deeply with a knife, it usually
bleeds; and she had never forgotten that, if you drink much from a
bottle marked “poison,” it is almost certain to disagree with you,
sooner or later.

However, this bottle was _not_ marked “poison,” so Alice ventured to
taste it, and finding it very nice, (it had, in fact, a sort of mixed
flavour of cherry-tart, custard, pine-apple, roast turkey, toffee, and
hot buttered toast,) she very soon finished it off.

*      *      *      *      *      *      *

    *      *      *      *      *      *

*      *      *      *      *      *      *


“What a curious feeling!” said Alice; “I must be shutting up like a
telescope.”

And so it was indeed: she was now only ten inches high, and her face
brightened up at the thought that she was now the right size for going
through the little door into that lovely garden. First, however, she
waited for a few minutes to see if she was going to shrink any further:
she felt a little nervous about this; “for it might end, you know,”
said Alice to herself, “in my going out altogether, like a candle. I
wonder what I should be like then?” And she tried to fancy what the
